entry: North American professional [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] league. The National Hockey League (NHL) comprises 32 teams, 25 in the [[United States]] and 7 in [[Canada]], and is considered the premier ice hockey league in the world. It was organized at the Windsor Hotel in [[Montreal]] on November 26, 1917, after the suspension of its predecessor, the National Hockey Association, and has been headquartered in [[New York City]] since 1989. The Stanley Cup, the oldest professional sports trophy in North America, is awarded annually to the playoff champion. Teams play 82 games each season, from October to April, and 16 teams advance to a four-round playoff. The [[Montreal Canadiens]] have won the most NHL titles, with 25. The Carolina Hurricanes won the 2026 Stanley Cup Final against the Vegas Golden Knights.

Art and history museum on the eastern side of [[Tiananmen Square]] in [[Beijing]]. Its building, completed in 1959, has a construction area of about 200,000 sq m and 48 exhibition halls, and it has the largest single building area of any museum in the world. Its collection of more than 1.4 million items includes the Houmuwu Ding, the heaviest piece of ancient bronzeware in the world at 832.84 kg, from the [[Shang dynasty]]. The museum reopened on March 17, 2011, after four years of renovation, with 28 new exhibition halls. It is a level-1 public welfare institution funded by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.

U.S. signals intelligence agency of the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]]. The National Security Agency (NSA) collects and processes global information for intelligence and counterintelligence, and protects U.S. communications networks. Originating as a World War II unit to decipher coded communications, it was formally established by President [[Harry S. Truman]] in 1952. Until the end of the [[Cold War]], it was the largest U.S. intelligence organization by personnel and budget. In 2013, [[Edward Snowden]] revealed secret surveillance programs. According to the leaked documents, the NSA intercepts and stores the communications of over a billion people worldwide.

Patriotic musical composition symbolizing the history and traditions of a [[Country|country]] or [[Nation|nation]]. Most national anthems are marches or [[Hymn|hymns]] in style. Some European monarchies adopted royal anthems in the [[Early modern period|early modern period]]. France adopted "La Marseillaise" as its national anthem by decree in 1795, making France the first country in history with an official national anthem. The Olympic Charter of 1920 introduced playing the anthems of gold medal winners, which gave nations without an official anthem an incentive to adopt one. The United States introduced "The Star-Spangled Banner" as its national anthem in 1931. Japan's anthem, "Kimigayo", took its lyrics from a [[Heian period]] poem but was not set to music until 1880.

Flag that represents and symbolizes a [[Nation|nation]], flown by its government and also by citizens. Flags originated as military standards, such as the white banners of the [[Zhou dynasty]]'s armies in the 11th century BC and the standards of the [[Roman Empire]]. Flying a national flag outside warfare became common with maritime flags. The [[Republic of Genoa]] was among the earliest states to adopt a national flag, according to William Gordon Perrin. The Dutch flag is perhaps the oldest tricolor in continuous use. The [[Union Jack]] originated with a royal decree of April 12, 1606, and took its current design on January 1, 1801, when the Cross of St. Patrick was added. The [[United States]] flag was first adopted as a naval ensign in 1777.

Nature park designated for conservation because of its unparalleled national natural, historic or cultural significance, and owned by a government. National parks are almost always accessible to the public and are usually developed, owned and managed by national governments. The United States established [[Yellowstone National Park]] in 1872; although it was not officially termed a national park at the time, it is widely held to be the first and oldest in the world. Parks Canada, established on May 19, 1911, is the world's oldest national park service. According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), 6,555 national parks worldwide met its criteria in 2006. The largest park meeting that definition is the [[Northeast Greenland National Park]], established in 1974 and covering 972,000 sq km.

Security and defense of a [[Sovereign state|sovereign state]], including its citizens, economy and institutions, regarded as a duty of government. Originally conceived as protection against military attack, national security now also includes non-military dimensions, such as protection from [[Terrorism|terrorism]], economic security and cyber security. Risks include actions by other states, violent nonstate actors, narcotic cartels, [[Organized crime|organized crime]], multinational corporations and natural disasters. Governments rely on political, economic and military power, as well as [[Diplomacy|diplomacy]], to safeguard the security of a state. They also act to reduce transnational causes of insecurity, such as [[Climate change|climate change]], [[Economic inequality|economic inequality]], political exclusion and nuclear proliferation. [[Walter Lippmann]] wrote in 1943 that a nation has security when it does not have to sacrifice legitimate interests to avoid war.

headword: Native Americans in the United States
sort_key: native americans in the united states
entry: Indigenous peoples of the [[United States]], particularly of the lower 48 states and [[Alaska]]. Following [[European colonization of the Americas]] from 1492, wars, enslavement and introduced diseases caused a precipitous decline in the population. The Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 ended recognition of independent Native nations, and the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted citizenship to Native Americans born in the U.S. Over five million Native Americans live in the United States, about 80% of them outside reservations. Many reservations remain independent of state law, and tribal citizens are subject only to tribal courts and federal law.

Japanese novelist, poet and scholar. He is considered one of the greatest writers in modern Japanese history and is often called the first modern novelist of Japan. His fiction explores individualism, loneliness and the conflict between traditional Japanese values and the rapid Westernization of the Meiji era. Major works include *I Am a Cat* (1905), *Botchan* (1906), *Sanshirō* (1908) and *Kokoro* (1914). A scholar of English literature, he taught at Tokyo Imperial University until 1907, when he became a full-time author for the *Asahi Shimbun*. He published a [[Novel|novel]] a year for the rest of his life, leaving his final work, *Light and Dark*, unfinished. His portrait appeared on the 1,000-yen banknote from 1984 to 2004.

Natural history museum in South Kensington, London. The museum holds some 80 million items in five main collections: botany, entomology, mineralogy, paleontology and zoology. They include specimens collected by [[Charles Darwin]]. It is a research center for [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomy]], identification and conservation. It is known for [[Dinosaur|dinosaur]] skeletons and ornate architecture; in 2017 a [[Diplodocus]] cast in the central hall was replaced by a [[Blue whale|blue whale]] skeleton hanging from the ceiling. The landmark Alfred Waterhouse building was built and opened by 1881. The museum was officially known as [[British Museum]] (Natural History) until 1992, although it had been legally separate from the British Museum since 1963. Like other publicly funded national museums in the United Kingdom, it charges no admission fee.

Living and nonliving things on Earth that occur naturally, without artificial human intervention. The term encompasses the interaction of all living species, [[Climate|climate]], weather and natural resources that affect human survival and economic activity. It is contrasted with the built environment, where humans have fundamentally transformed landscapes, as in urban settings and agricultural land conversion. No environment on Earth is absolutely natural, and naturalness varies along a continuum. Human changes in the [[Anthropocene]] have affected all natural environments, including through [[Climate change|climate change]], biodiversity loss and pollution from plastic and other chemicals. Earth science generally recognizes four spheres, corresponding to rocks, water, air and life: the [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]], [[Hydrosphere|hydrosphere]], [[Atmosphere|atmosphere]] and [[Biosphere|biosphere]]. Some scientists add the cryosphere and pedosphere.

Logarithm to the base of the mathematical constant [[E (mathematical constant)|e]], an irrational number approximately equal to 2.718. The natural logarithm of x, written ln x, is the power to which e must be raised to equal x; for example, ln 7.5 is 2.0149..., because e raised to that power equals 7.5. It is the inverse of the [[Exponential function|exponential function]] and turns multiplication into addition. It can be defined as the area under the curve y = 1/x from 1 to x for positive numbers. It is used to solve problems of exponential decay, such as [[Half-life|half-life]] calculations.

Systematic, research-based study of nature and the physical universe, ignoring [[Supernatural|supernatural]] influence. Used since at least [[Aristotle]] until the 19th century, the term referred to a branch of philosophy that included fields now considered science, such as physics, biology, chemistry and astronomy. Natural philosophy thus constitutes the theoretical and methodological foundations of modern science. [[Isaac Newton]]'s book *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687) reflects the use of the term in the 17th century. Jacopo Zabarella was the first person appointed as a specialist in natural philosophy, at the University of Padua in 1577. From the mid-19th century, natural philosophy came to mean just physics.

Branch of science concerned with the description, understanding and prediction of natural phenomena, based on empirical evidence from observation and experimentation. It is divided into two main branches: life science, also known as [[Biology|biology]], and physical science, which includes [[Physics|physics]], [[Astronomy|astronomy]], [[Earth science]] and [[Chemistry|chemistry]]. Natural science succeeded classical [[Natural philosophy|natural philosophy]]. It uses tools from mathematics and logic to convert information about nature into statements of natural laws. Systematic data collection succeeded natural history, which emerged in the 16th century by describing and classifying plants, animals and minerals. Mechanisms such as [[Peer review|peer review]] and reproducibility help ensure the validity of findings. [[Karl Popper]] proposed a controversial criterion of falsifiability to distinguish scientific endeavors from nonscientific ones.

Units of measurement based on universal physical constants. Stoney units, presented by George Johnstone Stoney in 1874, preceded Planck's by 30 years. Setting the speed of light c to 1 lets mass and energy be equated directly, so E = m rather than E = mc². A purely natural system has all of its dimensions collapsed, so the physical constants alone define the system. [[Planck units]] use the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant]], the [[Planck constant|reduced Planck constant]] and the [[Boltzmann constant]], and are common in theories of [[Quantum gravity|quantum gravity]], including [[String theory|string theory]]. Atomic units, first proposed by Douglas Hartree, are designed to simplify atomic and molecular physics, especially for the hydrogen atom. Geometrized units, used in [[General relativity]], set c and G to one.

Philosophical belief that only natural laws and forces, not [[Supernatural|supernatural]] ones, operate in the universe. In its strong form, metaphysical naturalism holds that spirits, deities and ghosts are not real. Philosophers often treat naturalism as equivalent to [[Materialism|materialism]] or physicalism, though important distinctions exist. Methodological naturalism is the more moderate view that naturalism should be assumed as the working paradigm, without judging whether it is true in the metaphysical sense. In the 20th century, Willard Van Orman Quine and George Santayana argued that scientific methods should also be used in philosophy. Western metaphysical naturalism originated in [[Ancient Greek philosophy]], among the atomists such as [[Democritus]].

British weekly international scientific journal. The journal publishes [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] research across the [[Natural science|natural sciences]], including biology, physics and chemistry, and is published by Springer Nature. Founded in 1869 by Norman Lockyer and Alexander MacMillan, it has editorial offices in London, the United States, continental Europe and Asia. Its 2022 impact factor of 50.5, from the Journal Citation Reports, was among the highest of multidisciplinary science journals. Fewer than 8% of submitted papers are accepted for publication. It also publishes news, commentary, features and sections on books and arts, as well as short [[Science fiction|science fiction]] stories. In 2007 it received the Prince of Asturias Award for Communications and Humanity, together with *Science*.

Lifestyle of practicing non-sexual social [[Nudity|nudity]] in private and in public, and the movement that advocates it. Naturism highlights an attitude favoring harmony with nature and respect for the environment, while nudism emphasizes the practice of nudity. Organizations emerged at the turn of the 20th century to promote social nudity and establish private campgrounds and resorts. Since the 1960s, clothing-optional public places have let people who do not identify as naturists take part in nude recreation. In 1974 the International Naturist Federation defined naturism as communal nudity intended to encourage self-respect, respect for others and respect for the environment.

Island country in [[Oceania]], in the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]]. Nauru lies within the [[Micronesia]] region, and at 21 sq km it is the third-smallest country in the world, with about 12,000 people. The island was annexed by the [[German Empire]] in the late 19th century and administered by Australia under a [[League of Nations]] mandate after World War I. Japan occupied it during World War II, and it became a [[United Nations]] trust territory before gaining independence from Australia in 1968. Mining its [[Phosphate|phosphate]], which stripped most of the interior from about 1900, brought wealth until reserves ran out in the 1990s, and mismanagement led to serious financial trouble in the 2000s. Since 2001 it has accepted Australian aid in exchange for hosting an offshore immigration detention facility. In 2026 it changed its official English name to Republic of Naoero.

Unit of length used in air, marine and space [[Navigation|navigation]] and for defining territorial waters. Historically, it was defined as one minute of [[Latitude|latitude]] along a meridian at the [[Equator]], so that Earth's polar circumference is very near 21,600 nautical miles. The international nautical mile is now exactly 1,852 meters (about 6,076 feet, or 1.151 miles). The derived unit of speed is the [[Knot (unit)|knot]], one nautical mile per hour. It is not part of the [[International System of Units]], but remains in common use because it corresponds to geographic [[Coordinate system|coordinates]]. Several symbols are in use, such as NM from the International Civil Aviation Organization.

Any of several [[Cephalopod|cephalopod]] species in the family Nautilidae, the sole living family in its superfamily. There are nine living species in two genera, with adult shells 10 to 25 cm in diameter. Coiled shells divided into chambers help control [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]]. Nautiluses have survived relatively unchanged for hundreds of millions of years and are often called "living fossils". Their tentacles, numbering 50 to over 90, lack suckers. Intensive trap fishing for shells has reduced populations, and all species are protected under CITES Appendix II.

Indigenous people of the Southwestern United States. The Navajo term for themselves is Diné, meaning "the people." Their language, *Diné bizaad*, is a Southern Athabaskan language closely related to Apache. Most Diné are enrolled in the [[Navajo Nation]], the second-largest federally recognized tribe, with more than 427,414 enrolled members as of 2026. Historically hunters and gatherers, the Navajo adopted farming from Pueblo peoples and herded [[Sheep|sheep]] and [[Goat|goats]] from the Spanish, which became a main source of trade and food. Women wove [[Wool|wool]] into blankets and clothing, and Navajo beadwork, painting and dress form a rich artistic tradition. Arizona and New Mexico hold more than three-quarters of the Diné population.

Native American reservation of the [[Navajo]] people, covering portions of northeastern [[Arizona]], northwestern [[New Mexico]] and southeastern [[Utah]]. At about 17,544,500 acres, it is the largest Native American reservation in the United States, larger than ten U.S. states. Its seat of government is in Window Rock, Arizona. The reservation was established in 1868 and reached its current boundaries in 1934. Its official language is Navajo, and tribal membership reached 399,494 in 2020, surpassing the Cherokee Nation.

Self-contained [[Explosive|explosive]] weapon placed in water to damage or destroy surface ships or [[Submarine|submarines]]. Left in place, it waits to be triggered by the approach of, or contact with, a vessel. Mines can be used offensively to hamper shipping or defensively to protect friendly sea lanes and harbors. Modern mines use high explosives and complex electronic fuzes, whereas early mines relied on [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] and physical ignition. Mines can be laid by aircraft, ships, submarines or individual swimmers. Producing and laying a mine usually costs between 0.5% and 10% of the cost of removing it, and clearing a minefield can take up to 200 times as long as laying one. Minesweeping is the practice of removing mines, usually with a specially designed minesweeper ship.

Combat in and on the sea, ocean or another major body of water. The armed forces branch for naval warfare is a [[Navy|navy]], and operations range from riverine (brown-water) to open-ocean (blue-water) applications. Humankind has fought battles at sea for more than 3,000 years. The first recorded sea battle, c. 1175 BC, saw the Egyptians defeat the [[Sea Peoples]] near the Nile Delta. For most of naval history, combat revolved around boarding and anti-boarding until the late 16th century, when the focus shifted to heavy ordnance. Many sea battles have left shipwrecks that aid underwater archaeology, including warships in the [[Pacific Ocean]]. For three centuries, [[Vikings]] raided far into central Russia and Ukraine, and even to distant [[Constantinople]].
